The Magazine of Magazines, September 1756
openalex_abstract: Front and back covers and pages from The Magazine of Magazines bound collection. In 1751, Limerick printer Andrew Welsh began printing an edition of the London based The Magazine of Magazines. Welsh, having learnt his trade from his father in Cork, began printing the Magazine, based in a building called ‘The Exchange’ on Nicholas Street, Englishtown, near the cathedral in Limerick. The Limerick publication started life as a direct, almost page for page, reprint of the London edition, printed by William Owen. The publication was a major undertaking for Welsh in Limerick. Welsh claims to have bought an entirely new set of type dedicated to printing the magazine, and the Limerick edition (like many other Irish re-prints of English works) is of better quality than its London counterpart. The Limerick edition was not simply aimed at the immediate urban public; there are three named retailers in Cork as well as one in Dublin. The Magazine, which was published for the best part of two decades, from 1751 to 1769, is a miscellany comprising of extracts from numerous eighteenth century periodicals and journals and covers subjects as diverse as Science, Philosophy, Medicine, Meteorology, Religion, Mythology and Literature to name but a few. It was the first periodical publication to feature Thomas Gray’s famous Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard, in 1751, and published essays and excerpts from towering intellectual figures of the day such as Dr Johnson and Voltaire. Prof Geraldine Sheridan, Dr. Michael Griffin, Yvonne Diggins, Research Assistant.

target_title: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas
openalex_display_name: Passing for American: Establishing American identity in the work of James Weldon Johnson, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Nella Larsen and Gertrude Stein.
openalex_abstract: Racial passing appears as a theme in both black- and white-authored American novels from the mid-nineteenth century on, and receives particularly intensive treatment during the 1920s. Since United States citizenship has by the early twentieth century come to mean an exceedingly rarefied whiteness, this dissertation argues that the establishment of any American citizen-identity in that period will inescapably proceed according to the model that passing provides. But racial categories are complex and shifting social phenomena. Thus I expand the concept of passing, arguing that Americans pass to escape whatever embodiment--race, gender, class, sexual orientation--obstructs their access to abstract American citizenship. Passing, that is, effectively disembodies one, so that one's operations in the public sphere will seem natural rather than transgressive. Thus I read as narratives of passing not just James Weldon Johnson's The Autobiography of an Ex-Coloured Man (1912) and Nella Larsen's Passing (1929), but also F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby (1925) and Gertrude Stein's The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas (1933). These texts deploy representations of passing so as to illuminate not just movement within, but alternative configurations of, the framework of national identity that would marginalize the overembodied subject. James Weldon Johnson creates a narrator whose mixed-race embodiment and decision to pass for white render him, ironically, a thoroughly representative American. Narrator Nick Carraway emphasizes that Gatsby's efforts to mingle with the polo-playing, Nordic upper class are strained and unnatural so as to avoid recognizing that he is himself passing. Irene Redfield's and Clare Kendry's radically divergent modes of passing in Larsen's novel reflect their distinct orientations to white patriarchal law. And Gertrude Stein reveals how passing both acquiesces in and undermines conventional identity at once, securing the social advantages of (an implicitly white and masculine) American identity by passing as a genius while conjuring through her concurrent passing performance as Alice a potentially infinite array of alternative configurations of the American subject.

openalex_display_name: Women's Poetry and Religion in Victorian England by Cynthia Scheinberg
openalex_abstract: This is a very timely publication. There has been a huge revival of interest in Victorian women's poetry in the last ten years, and it has led to a major reconfiguration of the English poetic landscape of the nineteenth century. Many of those feminist critics engaged in the recovery work of lost female voices from this period have had agendas far removed from the religious sphere. Yet religion and religious devotion were one of the major motivations driving many women poets towards publication of their work at a time when self-display of this kind was severely frowned on for women. Cynthia Scheinberg's excellent volume clearly demonstrates the importance of the religious element in the work of some of the most well-known of female poets, Christina Rossetti and Elizabeth Barrett Browning, where these elements have not been so much overlooked by earlier critics as perhaps, too homogeneously interpreted. For the angle introduced by Scheinberg is that of Jewish identity within Christian cultural formations in the Victorian period. She has chosen two poets from the mainstream Christian (Protestant) culture to compare with each other, and with two Anglo-Jewish poets, Amy Levy and Grace Aguilar. Her readings bring to light some unexpected and highly illuminating insights, and cast a different interpretation on some aspects that have previously been too quickly assimilated into a normative Christian reading. Scheinberg's research has taken her beyond the more obvious figures in the new canon of women poets; her chapter on the remarkable Jewish poet Amy Levy, and one on the less well-known Grace Aguilar, show an impressive breadth of research. Her work on Aguilar is particularly valuable as she is so little known -- and less understood, as an openly Jewish writer occupying space within a Christian tradition -- and I found the discussion of Aguilar's poetic project judicious and illuminating, having only known her previously through her best-selling Home Influence: A Tale for Mothers and Daughters (1847). Amy Levy's remarkably fine poetry has been taken up with avidity by critics anxious both to pay tribute to its understated intelligence, depth of feeling, and musicality and to decode the evidence of same-sex desires in pre-twentieth-century verse. Scheinberg accepts this evidence, but her extensive and finely tuned readings help to inflect the poetry towards another of its deeper interests, that of Jewish identity and its meaning for a young woman with a more problematic relation to her own Jewishness than Aguilar's, a relation which has often been traced in her novels -- specially the remarkable Reuben Sachs (1888) -- but seldom in her poetry -- until now. …

openalex_display_name: Musashi: from history to literature
openalex_abstract: Nascido por volta de 1583, Miyamoto Musashi se tornou uma figura de grande expressão da história japonesa, contribuindo com obras literárias, esculturas, projetos arquitetônicos, além de ser um dos maiores nomes japoneses da pintura em nanquim. Sua imagem foi explorada nas mais variadas mídias, que tendem a orbitar uma obra em especial: Musashi (1935-1939), romance escrito por Eiji Yoshikawa (1892-1962). O romance teve grande reflexo no processo de construção da identidade do Japão nos pós Primeira Guerra, bem como na maneira como o ocidente viria a idealizar aquela cultura. Em nosso trabalho, objetivamos demonstrar que a narrativa apresenta um hibridismo de gêneros, ao explorar elementos formais e estéticos próprios do modelo do romance histórico clássico e do romance de folhetim. Predomina, no entanto, o retorno aos elementos realistas da narrativa histórica do século XIX. Outrossim, analisamos a construção do protagonista do romance, demonstrando que Musashi se apresenta como um personagem híbrido, que reúne características do protagonista típico scottiano, do herói popular folhetinesco, assim como atributos que o aproximam dos heróis míticos. Contamos com o apoio teórico de Lukács (2011), Meyer (2005), Eco (1991) e Esteves (2010), dentre outros autores.

openalex_display_name: Dark, sad, depressing and perhaps pointless—yet another grant-earning award-winner for Australia!
openalex_abstract: Reviewed by: The Worry Front by H. C. Gildfind David C. Muller Dark, sad, depressing and perhaps pointless—yet another grant-earning award-winner for Australia! H. C. Gildfind. The Worry Front. Witchcliffe: Margaret River Press, 2017. A$24.99. 288 pp. ISBN 9780648027577 When reading a critically acclaimed collection of short stories penned by an author "with the support of the Australia Council Grant [that] includes [an] award-winning novella," one has to ask who decides that this particular writer or that this particular set of short stories is worthy of such magnanimous support. Who, in other words, decided that the short novella "Quarry" should win an award, and which award? (It is never mentioned anywhere in or on the book which award "Quarry" won or when). Though the cover blurbs—and there are three of them: two on the back cover, one on the front—use such complimentary phrases as "intense," "visceral" (which is used twice), as well as "surprising," "brilliant," "earthly," and "eloquently," these stories are—according to a blurb on the back cover—simultaneously "unsettling" and "macabre," so much so that a second reading of this collection will not likely be forthcoming. Many of Gildfind's stories are indeed unsettling. They are also sad and unnerving. Many of them did not induce feelings of happiness, nor were many of these stories entertaining. Literature—and what qualifies as good literature that is worthy of an award—is a concept lost on many regular readers or, as some prefer to call them, those little people out there who turn published novels into commercially successful blockbusters. When a collection like this comes along, and the stories and the novella are consumed, the taste left behind for the reader—or at least this reader—is not one of satisfaction. Put another way: what exactly is the point of Gildfind's collection, which—so we are told—is "reminiscent of [Virginia] Woolf or [Katherine] Mansfield," when the content of these stories is off-putting, dreary, or even sour? The first story in The Worry Front, "Ferryman," sets the overall tone for this collection. As is the case with many of Gildfind's stories, it is not immediately clear or obvious that this first story does not actually take place in Australia, a plot point slowly revealed by this story's icy setting. The style of writing in "Ferryman," as near as it can be discerned, is a type of first-person stream of consciousness, yet the content of [End Page 171] the story is categorically dark: the unnamed protagonist is accused of some type of rape or sexual molestation, and there is a subplot that features a father-like figure, hunting, and some birds, all of which are ultimately rounded off by the discovery of a dead baby in a discarded nylon bag. The second story—the collection's titular "The Worry Front"—focuses on an eighty-year-old widow who, in an extreme bout of depression, looks back on her life at a time when she worried about her children in a manner similar to the advent of a weather phenomenon or, in this case, a "worry front," hence the story's title. This widow comes to realize that her children have grown into mean and unhappy adults, so she puts her dead husband's cat to sleep after methodically swallowing a month's worth of ball bearings, thumbtacks, and other small metallic objects. All of this is ahead of an MRI procedure that will presumably activate the metals inside her body in an attempt to induce suicide by way of medical-device magnetism. Focus quickly shifts to poultry in the third entry, "Gently, Gently," a story about two men, one of whom builds a chicken coop for three egg-laying hens. The story is narrated in the first person by an unnamed narrator; the other man in the story gets drunk and shatters a glass door. He is later sent to the hospital while the first man—the one who built the chicken coop at the start of the story—relocates an escaped chicken that he returns to the coop. openalex_display_name: Affective Mapping: Melancholia and the Politics of Modernism by Jonathan Flatley (review)
openalex_abstract: Reviewed by: Affective Mapping: Melancholia and the Politics of Modernism by Jonathan Flatley Denise Ginfray Jonathan Flatley. Affective Mapping: Melancholia and the Politics of Modernism. Cambridge: Harvard UP, 2008. 263pp. In this brilliant contribution to the studies of modernism, concerned with “a particular mode of modernist melancholizing” (2), the author [End Page 857] investigates the concept of loss central to Freud’s theory developed in “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), choosing to combine individual histories of melancholia and loss, collective consciousness, ideology, culture, and the different predicaments of modernity. Jonathan Flat-ley’s “historical-aesthetic methodology” (3), with its many references to prominent theoretical works, is grounded on his dynamic concept of “Affective mapping,” namely “the aesthetic technology—in the older, more basic sense of a techne—that represents the historicity of one’s affective experience” (4). This book convincingly articulates theory and practice: in addition to a very useful glossary devoted to the key concepts of this essay (“Affect, Emotion, Mood [Stimmung], Structure of Feeling” [11–24]), two chapters describe the complex theoretical framework in detail, and the last three chapters offer a critical reading of three major literary narratives: Henry James’s The Turn of The Screw (1898), W. E. B. Du Bois’s Souls of Black Folk (1903), and Andrei Platonov’s Chevengur (1926–1930). In his introduction, where he posits that the modern subject is shaped by the social and historical forces of collective experience through emotions, Flatley claims the necessity to regard the mapping process as experimental and “revisable” (7), and “the map” in relation to the Deleuzean concept of “rhizome.” The reader will certainly appreciate how carefully the author delineates his critical tools in his glossary, insisting on the similarities and differences between “emotion” (“something that happens inside and tends toward outward expression” [12]), “affects” (“always experienced in relation to an object or objects” [16]), “mood” (“a kind of affective atmosphere” [19]), and “structure of feeling” (“the ways social forces shape or structure our affective lives” [24]). Flatley develops his critical perspective in chapter 1 “Modernism and Melancholia”, and in chapter 2 “Affective Mapping”: borrowing mainly from Freud, Benjamin, Heidegger, Adorno, and Jameson, he suggests that the modern relation to time and temporality, the overwhelming influence of science and technology, the many discourses of normalization, have all created the melancholic subject. But, the critic insists, the aesthetic enterprise offers a response to depression: by distancing both the creative stance and his receptor from the entropic zone of loss and mourning, the imaginary scene of literature, among other forms of artistic experiences, may become a site where affects are rearticulated and recontextualized in a positive way, following a logic similar to the transferential logic of psychoanalysis. In chapter 3, “Reading into Henry James: Allegories of the Will to Know in The Turn of the Screw,” Flatley examines how “the ghosts from our past” (89) shape the reader’s experience and how the subtle dialectic between possession and dispossession affects [End Page 858] audiences. The critic considers Freud’s concept of tranference to be an essential component of James’s aesthetic venture in this novella. In addition, with reference to Michel Foucault and to the will to know that underlies the politics of modern sexuality, he argues that the embedded narratives of James’s work provide an emotional pattern of interpretation dominated by libidinal desire turned into textual energy. It is also relevant to relate the publication of The Turn of the Screw to its historical context, for the latter radically shaped the nature and function of creative imagination and altered the tenets of artistic commitment. Flatley insists on the historicity of James’s aesthetic, and he notes how, at the moment when epistemological doubt ushered the Western world into modernity, the novelist’s theory of reading responded to the collective sense of despondency by mapping individual affects and emotions into a shared experience of defamiliarization. James was genuinely convinced that “mimesis, possession, confusions of self and other and past and present—in a word ghosts—are necessary for life” (102). It is precisely this dominant mode of spectrality that combines pleasure, desire for the narrative, and imaginary identifications that so strongly appeals to most of us...

openalex_display_name: Kate Chopin's 'The Awakening' and the Exploration of Feminine Desire and Expression
openalex_abstract: In ‘ The Awakening’ , Kate Chopin introduces Edna Pontellier, the wife of a New Orleans businessman and as a mother of two children. Despite her conventional roles, Edna struggles with romantic feelings and sexual desires to gain her own independence. In search of true self and genuine desires of her own, Edna defies social conventions on her journey of self-discovery. Her previous submissive life is transformed into a radically subversive one. Her newly awakened feminine desires find expression in her paintings. Edna’s desires and voice are powerful enough to overcome patriarchal culture and its expectations regarding women’s role. Her paintings become her only subversive tool to inscribe her awakened desires. In the novel, Chopin implicitly suggests that feminine expression which is embodied in Edna’s paintings is a necessary tool to free Edna from conventional roles as a mother or wife.

openalex_display_name: The Strange Career of Ulysses S. Grant
openalex_abstract: The Strange Career of Ulysses S. Grant Owen Wister (bio) OWEN WISTER (1860–1938) is now best known as the author of The Virginian, a novel published in 1902 and one of the founding documents in the enduring and endlessly evolving conception of the American frontier in general and the western hero in particular. The grandson of Fanny Kemble, one of the most celebrated actresses of the nineteenth century, he was born in Philadelphia, educated in boarding schools in Europe and the United States, and graduated summa cum laude from Harvard in 1882. His early ambitions centered on music (Franz Liszt heard him play and confirmed his achievements), but he returned to Philadelphia to undertake a career in business at the same time as he pursued a series of writing projects. The strain produced by these conflicting imperatives likely resulted in a nervous breakdown, and in 1885 he traveled to Wyoming—the first of many such trips to that region—in hopes of restoring his health. After securing a degree from the Harvard Law School, he committed himself to a life as a writer of western fiction, publishing a sequence of stories and novels on this theme over the decade from 1891 to 1902. Two years before the appearance of The Virginian, an enormously successful book that would continue to hold the attention of readers for generations, Wister published a brief biography of Ulysses S. Grant in the series of Beacon Biographies of Eminent Americans edited by Mark De Wolfe Howe. In later years there were some comparable works: The Seven Ages of Washington came out in 1907 and Roosevelt: The Story of a Friendship, which traced his association with Theodore Roosevelt back to their years together at Harvard, appeared in 1930. Over the course of the last three decades of his life, Wister's work moved in different directions—he brought out a novel of social manners, Lady Baltimore (1906), reminiscent of Henry James, who was a friend of his mother's, as well as a variety of political writings; but he was drawn again and again to the western, which— however uneasy he might have been about the literary confinement associated with that genre—seemed to offer him a necessary imaginative home. As for General and later President Ulysses S. Grant, his complex career, alternating between personal failure and public success, has continued to haunt the minds of readers and writers ever since the publication of his Memoirs, one of the greatest works of American autobiography ever written. F. Scott Fitzgerald's Tender Is the Night is only one of the works that reflects its deep and lasting impact and the vexing nature of Grant's ambiguous example. This excerpt from Owen Wister's short life of Grant is taken from his Ulysses S. Grant in the Beacon series, published in 1900 by Small, Maynard & Company in Boston. —SD [End Page 197] None of our public men have a story so strange as this. It is stranger than Lincoln's. It is very much the strangest of them all. ________ Is it accident that at the beginning of a certain four years this middle-aged man should be nobody, and at the end should be the one commander out of all to win and retain the supreme confidence of his government and his people? It has been called accident by some grown-up writers. His own words give the unconscious explanation: "I feel as sure of taking Richmond as I do of dying." Not McClellan, not Meade, not Lincoln himself, not any one at all, had ever been able to feel as sure as that. This utter certainty of the Union's success burned in Grant like a central fire, and, with all his limitations, made his will a great natural force which gravitated simply and irresistibly to its end. The Mountain Came Long Ago to Mohammed: The American Cultural Invasion of Mexico as Seen in the Short Fiction of Maria Cristina Mena
openalex_abstract: Maria Cristina Mena holds a unique place in American literature: She is the first naturalized American from Mexico to write in English and publish in prestigious American magazines. Born on April 3, 1893, in Mexico City to a politically powerful and socially prominent family of Spanish extraction, Mena lived the life of a privileged young lady, being educated at the elite convent school in the Mexican capital, Hijas de Maria (Daughters of Mary), and later at an English boarding school. An unusually intelligent, sensitive, and perceptive child, she began to write poetry when she was ten years old. As the result of the political turmoil in Mexico during the first decade of the twentieth century, Mena was sent at the age of fourteen to live with family friends in New York City. There she continued her studies and began to write in earnest. She was twenty when her first two short stories were published in November of 1913: John of God, the Water-Carrier in Century Magazine and The Gold Vanity Set in American Magazine. By 1916, Mena had published a total of eight stories and one biographical essay. John of God was reprinted in the October 1927 issue of Monthly Criterion, a literary journal published in London and edited by T. S. Eliot. Edward O'Brien selected the work for his volume of Best Short Stories of 1928. In 1916, she married a divorce6 twenty-six years her senior, Henry Kellett Chambers, a respected Australian-born playwright and senior editor and columnist for the Literary Digest. couple traveled in literary circles and counted D.H. Lawrence and Aldous Huxley among their friends. Chambers died in 1935, leaving Mena, much to her surprise, totally destitute. For nearly twenty years, they had lived an exciting if expensive life of elegance in a mansion on Long Island Sound. But with the death of her husband, Dona Marfa, as she now preferred to be called, became a virtual recluse. She was forty-two years old and penniless, forced by circumstance to move from Long Island to Brooklyn, where she lived for the remainder of her life on the charity of friends in a series of dingy apartments, ending up living alone in a cold-water flat, along with the ashes of her beloved husband which she kept in a coffee-can and guarded under her bed. When she did venture out, it was to attend the regular meeting of the Catholic Library Association and the Authors Guild of New York. At such meetings, she was able to continue her friendships with editors, librarians, educators, and other writers such as Clare Booth Luce, Theodore Maynard, and Wilfred Sheed and where she made new friends such as Covelle Newcomb, a promising young writer from San Antonio. Mena continued to write children's novels publishing five books between 1942 and 1953, but they are mostly reworkings of her short stories. She died a pauper in Brooklyn on August, 3, 1965, cremated and buried with funds provided with funds supplied by her stepson, whom she never saw during her life. Fifteen people attended the funeral. period between 1900 and 1930 saw a great influx of Mexicans into the United States, many of them, like Mena, fleeting the turmoil of the Mexican revolution that began in 1910. During those early years in New York and even later, Mena dedicated herself to giving American readers vivid and true portraits of the many faces of the many Mexicos. As T.S. Eliot noted when he re-published John of God in 1927, Maria Cristina Mena had perhaps the most comprehensive series of stories of Mexican life published in English. In her stories, she touches on the lives of the religious and the sacrilegious, the faithful and the hypocritical, the industrious and the lazy, the wise and the gullible as well as the native and the foreign (Simmen, 39-40). Curiously enough, considering that the stories were written at the turn of the twentieth century, two of the themes most prominent in her fiction are both current and meaningful. …

openalex_display_name: Walt Whitman and the Making of Jewish American Poetry
openalex_abstract: One of my happiest memories as a Walt Whitman scholar was having lunch with Gerald Stern and Philip Levine when my colleague, the novelist Ruth Knafo Setton, had invited them to give a joint poetry reading for the Philip and Muriel Berman Center for Jewish Studies at Lehigh University. In a brief conversation with Stern, the topic turned to Whitman’s last days in Camden, New Jersey, and I mentioned that Whitman’s final words to his caretaker Warren “Warry” Fritzinger were “Shift, Warry”—a request to move his aging body into a more comfortable position on his deathbed. Stern immediately turned to Levine to tell him the story about Whitman’s final words. At the time, I fondly thought that one or the other of these titans of American poetry would end up writing a poem that included this bit of Whitman lore. (Neither ever did, as far as I know.) After reading Dara Barnat’s excellent new book Walt Whitman and the Making of Jewish American Poetry, however, I have a better understanding of how this casual exchange was part of a larger pattern.Barnat’s central argument has two major components. The first is that Walt Whitman (1819–92) provides a “generational” influence on Jewish American poets through “thematic and formalistic” inspiration (24). This lineal descent from Whitman’s sprawling, free-verse poetry is clear in Adrienne Rich’s An Atlas of the Difficult World (1991) or Allen Ginsberg’s Howl and Other Poems (1956), just as Whitman’s democratic ethos is apparent in the work of Karl Shapiro and Kenneth Koch. But in addition to tracing this genealogical lineage, Barnat makes a second, more complex argument about Whitman’s role within a larger network of “poets who write of straddling Jewish and American culture(s), negotiating notions of and conflicts around Jewish identity” (24). Barnat reconstructs this network around a few key nodes—Whitman’s legacy within high modernism is one of them—such that “any response by a Jewish American poet to Whitman can be read in relation to this network of poets, which stretches as much backward into the past as it does forward into the future” (24). It was this network of Jewish American poets connected to each other by way of Whitman that I witnessed firsthand when Gerald Stern told Philip Levine the “Shift, Warry” story over lunch.By arguing that Whitman played a central role in the making of Jewish American poetry, Barnat is working within familiar territory. Whitman’s towering influence has been a commonplace of American literary history since the first decades of the twentieth century, with texts as early as D. H. Lawrence’s Studies in Classic American Literature (1923) making the case for Whitman’s singular impact on the poets who come after him. The late twentieth century similarly gave us academic monographs such as James E. Miller Jr.’s The American Quest for a Supreme Fiction: Whitman’s Legacy in the Personal Epic (1979), Neeli Cherkowsi’s Whitman’s Wild Children (1988, with an expanded edition in 1999), and Thomas Gardner’s Discovering Ourselves in Whitman: The Contemporary American Long Poem (1989). A standout publication in this list is the Jim Perlman, Ed Folsom, and Dan Campion edition Walt Whitman: The Measure of His Song, an indispensable collection of poets’ responses to Whitman that was first published in 1981 and later updated in both 1998 and 2019.This critical project to document Whitman’s influence on subsequent generations of poets is ongoing, as evidenced by recent work such as Catherine Davies’s Whitman’s Queer Children: America’s Homosexual Epics (2012), B. A. Van Sise’s Children of the Grass: A Portrait of American Poetry (2019), and Caroline Chamberlin Hellman’s Children of the Raven and the Whale: Visions and Revisions in American Literature (2019). Barnat’s Walt Whitman and the Making of Jewish American Poetry is a welcome addition to this body of work, both for the analysis of individual poets that it provides and for the larger model of networked literary influence that it offers. Similarly valuable is her argument that, in addition to influencing Jewish American poets, Whitman himself is retroactively transformed by these poets’ engagement with his life and work. Barnat writes, “Whitman as an American poet shapes Jewish poetry and Jewish poets in America, in turn, shape Walt Whitman” (31). These two distinctive contributions—a networked model of literary history and a bidirectional model of influence—make Barnat’s book a standout in this scholarly tradition.Following a tight yet thorough overview of Whitman’s reception by Jewish American poets since the nineteenth century, Barnat’s first chapter, “Charles Reznikoff, the Jewish Objectivist Poets, and Walt Whitman,” introduces one of the key elements of her larger argument regarding the legacy of high modernism. Barnat singles out Reznikoff as a representative figure among a larger group of other early twentieth-century Objectivist poets who “embraced Whitman, despite being closely entwined with Ezra Pound and other high modernist poets, who often held complicated attitudes toward Whitman” and often expressed “anti-Jewish sentiments” (25). Barnat demonstrates how Reznikoff drew on Whitmanian themes and forms, such as the trope of the urban poet walking through the streets of New York City. Some readers might take issue with Barnat’s claims that a given Reznikoff poem is either directly or indirectly referencing Whitman’s urban flaneur from poems such as “Faces” or “Song of Myself,” but the larger thrust of her argument is not that one poem gave birth to another; rather, she argues that literary influence is best understood within a broader network of both aesthetic and cultural forces. She writes, “The extent to which Whitman is intrinsic to Reznikoff’s work is more meaningful within the literary, historical, and political background of Ezra Pound’s often anti-Whitman and exclusionary High Modernist setting” (51). As such, these “allusions to Whitman are markers of identity as Jewish American poets writing amid High Modernism” (51).Barnat’s second chapter, “Whitman versus High Modernists: On Karl Shapiro and Kenneth Koch,” follows closely on the first in its analysis of how Whitman serves as an anchor point for Jewish American poets engaging with the legacy of high modernism. Some of the most compelling examples that Barnat cites come from a handful of essays written by Shapiro that pit Whitman against figures such as T. S. Eliot and Ezra Pound. “It can be argued that The Waste Land and even the Cantos are redactions of Leaves of Grass,” writes Shapiro in one such essay, while in another he questions “Hart Crane’s identification with the sense of Whitman, while rejecting the revolutionary forms” (qtd. in 59–60). Barnat makes the case that Shapiro uses Whitman against high modernism not only because “Whitman’s pluralistic vision threatens [modernist] poets’ elitist culture” (60) but also because Shapiro’s sense of himself as an “exile” within American culture connects him with Whitman’s own outsider status as “one of the roughs.” This is where Barnat’s argument about Shapiro and Whitman’s shared outsider status—as prophetic voices crying in the wilderness—gets interesting. She writes, “By understanding Whitman as a prophetic poet, presumably like any of the Jewish prophets of the Bible with extraordinary knowledge and insight, Shapiro positions Whitman in a Jewish context,” a move, she argues, that turns “Whitman into a prophetic poet and thus a quasi-Jew” (61–62). The argument here is not that Whitman becomes Jewish when he enters Shapiro’s domain so much as it is that Whitman facilitates an engagement with Jewish identity among a network of poets. Barnat’s discussion of how Kenneth Koch reacts to both Whitman and Shapiro makes this point eloquently: “Koch’s Jewish American identity informs a reading of his responses to Whitman within the context of Shapiro’s and the wide network of Jewish American poets from the mid-nineteenth century” onward (66).The third chapter, “Whitman’s Poetics of Witness: Muriel Rukeyser, Allen Ginsberg, and Gerald Stern,” further details Whitman’s function in a networked literary history as Barnat writes of poets who “turn to each other when it comes to Whitman (Ginsberg to Reznikoff, Stern to Ginsberg, and Adrienne Rich, Alizia Ostriker, and Marge Piercy to Rukeyser)” (78). The payoff in how Barnat situates Ginsberg within this broader network is particularly rewarding, as Ginsberg’s homages to Whitman in poems such as “A Supermarket in California” (1956) are arguably the most well known in American poetry. Barnat’s contention is that “Ginsberg’s affiliation to Whitman was not isolated” to a relationship between the two poets but was a part of Ginsberg’s response to Reznikoff, Reznikoff’s engagement with Whitman, and all three poets’ entanglement with high modernism. Barnat makes a similar argument about Stern (“[T]he Jewish Whitman that Stern receives has roots in Ginsberg and in the Objectivist-Modernist legacy of Reznikoff, Pound, and Williams” [28]), whereas her focus on Rukeyser is more forward-looking. Rukeyser appropriates Whitman to position herself “in relation to her Jewish American identity” (79) while also providing a future foundation for the women poets Barnat discusses in her fourth chapter.Chapter 4, “Jewish American Women Poets Respond to Walt Whitman: Adrienne Rich, Alicia Ostriker, and Marge Piercy,” describes how Rukeyser serves as the “guiding foremother” of late twentieth-century poets who approach Whitman “in radically complex and often contradictory ways: as a figure of poetic and personal liberation, as a feminist ally, and no less as a symbol of an ailing, failing (or already failed) America” (29). This chapter is less thematically consistent than some of the others in the book, but there are good reasons for this approach. These poets’ responses to Whitman are consistent with the pattern that Barnat describes throughout the book—in that connections with Whitman involve multiple, networked connections with other Jewish American poets (particularly Rukeyser)—but their various engagements with him differ both from one another and across the arc of individual careers. Broadly speaking, Rich draws on Whitman to navigate her relationship with American politics and her Jewish identity, whereas Ostriker is more focused on politics and Piercy on her spiritual inheritances from Judaism.In a brief conclusion chapter, Barnat points toward a number of other poets who could also be placed within a networked literary history of Whitman and Jewish American poets: C. K. Williams, Jerome Rothenberg, and Charles Bernstein. Whether or not future scholars choose to pursue further study in this area, Barnat has provided an excellent model for how to engage with major figures such as Whitman in compelling new ways.

openalex_display_name: A Son at the Front; American Writers and World War I
openalex_abstract: Wharton scholars will warmly welcome this attractive new edition of Wharton’s war novel in the centenary year of its original publication. Oxford World’s Classics has been producing excellent and affordable editions of novels with informative notes and introductory essays for over one hundred years. However, this is the first time since 2015 that there has been a new addition to their offerings of Wharton’s novels. It is, therefore, of some considerable import that A Son at the Front has been added to The House of Mirth, Ethan Frome, The Custom of the Country, The Age of Innocence, and Summer. In contrast to these other well-known novels, A Son at the Front has not received anywhere near the same attention and acclaim. It was only in 2015, during the centenary commemorations of the First World War, that the Library of America added it to its Wharton portfolio, with notes by Hermione Lee, in a volume containing four of Wharton’s novels published in the 1920s.Julie Olin-Ammentorp has long championed Wharton’s war fiction and her 2004 publication, Edith Wharton’s Writings from the Great War, made a significant contribution to Wharton scholarship. Citations alone testify to its authoritative status. A Son at the Front was for many decades overlooked by literary scholars with the tenacious canonization of texts that subscribed to what Samuel Hynes characterized as the “Myth of War” approach. The broadening of the appreciation of different and sometimes contradictory responses to the war from both combatant and noncombatant authors has provided a more comprehensive platform for considering Wharton’s contribution, and reading the novel in 2023 may just prompt a reassessment of the text.In her introductory essay, Olin-Ammentorp refers to the current war in Ukraine and this does give readers a contemporary framework for understanding Wharton’s description of the disruption war caused back in 1914 to civilians’ plans of travel and to supplies of food and fuel. We might also add similarities in the rhetoric of the need to defend democracy, western civilization, national sovereignty, human rights, and international law with particular regard to war crimes. We could further add how non-Ukrainians—many by going to Ukraine—have been stirred to respond to the plight of refugees, the need to evacuate Ukrainians from areas under siege, and, of course, the need for professional soldiers. In addition, there have been concerted efforts by the European Union and other countries to support Ukrainian culture and its artists. What this tells us is that Wharton’s novel transcends its immediate context and speaks to prominent elements in the representation of war and its impact on life. It contributes to discussions about how to represent conflict, polarization, and propaganda. As such, Wharton’s novel should not only be seen in the context of World War I writings but also in the general context of the war novel.The annotations to this edition of A Son at the Front are more fulsome than the Library of America edition. Inevitably publishers must consider word count, but there is another issue here that is worth raising. Some annotations lend themselves more easily to a so-called factual accounting. Some of those annotations are particularly pertinent with regard to the increasingly distant nature of the novel’s setting and the current time of the reader. However, Wharton’s allusions to a work of art or literature, at the very least, can never be taken at face value. She routinely played with her broad swath of allusions to western cultural traditions and these stretch right across her entire oeuvre. Much of this has to do with her sense of continuity and tradition, and with locating her work within a far larger context. She straddled the need to sell books and her aspiration to be a serious writer of fiction whose work would stand the test of time. The contemporary reviews of A Son at the Front demonstrate only too clearly how reviewers were caught up in the moment and failed to appreciate the mind at work in searching for a way to represent wartime experiences. Readers should therefore not stop at an annotation that provides them with sources and information. Take, for example, how Wharton slips in a reference to Milton’s poem, “Lycidas,” with the phrase “the tangles of Neara’s hair” or her comparison of the coils of a telephone to the serpents coiled around Laocoön. There is so much to be gained from following these up and realizing the intricate playfulness of Wharton’s allusions and how this can influence the interpretation of her novels. Some of her ironic tone can be entirely missed without an appreciation of what she alludes to and how she does so.Olin-Ammentorp’s introductory essay provides a comprehensive survey of the writing and reviews of A Son at the Front, as well as its place in Wharton’s overall oeuvre and in World War I novels. The section on “Seeing Paris” draws attention to how the war is refracted through the eyes of an American expatriate and portrait artist, John Campton. As Olin-Ammentorp points out, he is a difficult protagonist for readers to identify with. This is a gamble on Wharton’s part, given what she wrote in “The Vice of Reading” about the proclivities of the “mechanical reader,” but it also negates any sentimentality. Wharton’s choice, therefore, of this protagonist as her “reflecting mind” enabled her to provide a satirical depiction of the superficiality of some American expatriates’ war efforts. While her representation fits in with her earlier critiques of society figures and their motivations for their display of wealth and philanthropy, there was little in this novel to offer them solace regarding the role of individuals in the “strange war-world of the rear,” let alone the US government prior to the declaration of war. On the other hand, it offered an opportunity for introspection about international outreach and the role of the United States in global affairs, having been published at a time when isolationist rhetoric began to crescendo.There is a further aspect to consider with regard to how Campton sees Paris in wartime. This has to do with Walt Whitman’s descriptions of Washington, DC, at the time of the Civil War. We are alerted to the connection between these and what Wharton portrays in her novel with the prominent positioning of the epigraph, drawn from Whitman’s Specimen Days. There are numerous allusions to Whitman in Wharton’s work and it is worth going beyond the obvious connection in this instance—namely, the way in which Wharton picks up on Whitman’s observations of combatants and the way in which “they are different from the rest . . . ‘something odd about them’” and their tendency to “go off and meditate and muse in solitude” (48). Consider, for example, how Whitman describes Washington, DC, in the moonlight or gaslight and Campton’s “painter’s vision” of the illuminations in the Place de la Concorde and how the light lies on the city in “wide silvery washes” (130). Is there not a possibility that Wharton is prompting the reader to compare Whitman and Campton and their response to the devasting wars in their lifetime? On one hand, there is the two artists’ similar response to light and shape and forms, and on the other, there is a stark contrast between Whitman and Campton. The poet fully embraced the need to visit wounded and dying soldiers in various army hospitals, whereas Campton recoils from hospital visits unless they are to see his son. The contrast underscores Campton’s misanthropic and selfish disposition. If, as Campton insists at the beginning, this is not his son’s war to fight, then it is not America’s war to fight. But Campton undergoes a transformation and stands in for the change in position that Woodrow Wilson’s administration undertook to shift from neutrality to engagement. This pivot was crucial to the increase in the Allies’ military advantage and to the fractious debate within the United States thereafter about the nation’s global role. As such, this makes Wharton’s novel of particular interest to both the history and the ongoing debate of US involvement overseas.There are many reasons to take a new look at Wharton’s novel and to reappraise it. Julie Olin-Ammentorp’s work and her achievement in getting Oxford University Press to publish a scholarly edition of Wharton’s 1923 novel should inspire new efforts. David A. Rennie’s American Writers and World War I provides an overview of a select number of authors who published fiction featuring the Great War. He devotes a chapter to Wharton, to Ellen La Motte together with Mary Borden, to Thomas Boyd, to F. Scott Fitzgerald, to Laurence Stallings, and to Ernest Hemingway. This selection, Rennie argues, is “representative of the diverse influences of World War I on American authors,” who also dealt with the war in several other genres that have garnered less critical attention. He provides a good amount of context for each author and compares them in terms of their relationship to the war, of their writing careers, and of their experience of the publishing industry. Unlike other recent volumes covering a variety of American authors who produced war fiction in the early twentieth century, Rennie probes well beyond the immediate time of the writing and publication of war novels with which the authors are most associated. This provides an opportunity to see their war-related fiction in terms of their overall oeuvre and, more pointedly, to examine how their perspectives on the war may have evolved from 1918 onwards. Wharton scholars will find of particular interest the juxtaposition of Wharton with these other authors, including those long regarded as part of the Lost Generation, and how this enables readers to contextualize her complex and sometimes contradictory responses to the war. Rennie rigorously resists any simplistic and static categorization of individual authors’ reactions, hence the title of his introductory chapter: “The Hell with All the Dirty, Easy Labels”, a quote from F. Scott Fitzgerald. Drawing upon the work of scholars such as Hazel Hutchison and Steven Trout, Rennie draws attention to the struggles that novelists had with making sense of the war, the sacrifice of millions of lives, and the destruction of the built environment and countryside. This volume is firmly located among the work of those who have sought to broaden the field beyond the canonical texts that were predominant in the literary curriculum and anthologies up until thirty or so years ago.Much of Rennie’s coverage is dependent on existing scholarship on individual authors and does not necessarily cover new ground. Wharton scholars, therefore, will not find much in the chapter on Wharton that has not already been covered by Alan Price and Julie Olin-Ammentorp. Rennie’s coverage does not go into great depth and the analysis of Wharton’s war writings is brief. To be fair, the focus is on contexts rather than texts. He emphasizes her Francophilia to the exclusion of her wider knowledge and use of the western literary tradition, particularly with regard to the literary representation of war. Curiously, he omits her use of Whitman in her epigraph for the novel, while pointing to Borden taking inspiration from Whitman’s “A Song of Myself.” The Book of the Homeless is given a section, but there is no analysis of its content or links to her work with refugees or the depiction of “murdered houses” in Fighting France. In Morocco is absent and there is a missed opportunity here to draw a comparison with La Motte. With regard to the latter, Rennie provides a valuable insight into the relationship of the text she wrote during the war following a year’s tour of Southeast Asia criticizing European colonialism with her Backwash of the War and its questioning of the extolling of fighting for liberty, justice, and civilization.As an introduction to American writers and the First World War, Rennie’s book provides a useful overview of seven authors with different experiences of the war and at different stages in their careers, united by their multifaceted and evolving responses to the conflagration. It will enable readers to have a broader appreciation of that part of the American literary community which was, like Wharton, intensely engaged with the war and its impact, and, more importantly, it will encourage readers to make further comparisons.

Metropolitan novels like Henry James's The Bostonians (1886), E. M. Such instances provides insistent—if frequently unrecognized—reminders that these urban centers are shaped by plantation colonialism, agriculture, labor, culture, and ideology. Joyce's work has been thoroughly examined from postcolonial perspectives, including its influence on West Indian writers like Derek Walcott.3 Such criticism does not explicitly consider Joyce's fiction in relation to transnational, national, or regional plantation cultures. Situating Joyce within a network of plantation modernists brings him into dialogue with a range of both metropolitan and colonial writers in ways that go beyond implicitly hierarchical models of influence. My comparative plantation framework puts Joyce on equal footing with writers from throughout the global plantation complex to reveal shared aesthetic and political concerns at work in his fiction. Within this context, Stephen Dedalus's famous declaration "History … is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake" resonates with Faulkner's assertion that "The past is never dead. This literature includes early official histories of plantation colonialism from metropolitan perspectives like Edmund Spenser's A View of the Present State of Ireland (1633) and Médéric Louis Élie Moreau de Saint-Méry's history of Saint Domingue (1789). It also includes nineteenth-century romances like Maria Edgeworth's Castle Rackrent (1800), William Earle's Obi; or, the History of Three-Fingered Jack (1800), Victor Hugo's Bug-Jargal (1826), and Thomas Nelson Page's In Ole Virginia (1887). openalex_display_name: Dialogism and Carnival in Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse: A Bakhtinian Reading
openalex_abstract: Mikhail Bakhtin's dialogism in a novel promises the creation of a domain of interactive context for different voices which results in a polyphonic discourse. Instead of trying to suppress each other, the voices of the novel interact upon the other voices in a way that none of them tries to silent the other ones, and each one has the opportunity to express itself. In Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse , although some voices attempt to be more dominant, all are allowed to be heard and interact with the other ones. In this way Mrs. Ramsay acts like a link that helps to create a dialogic discourse by respecting the voices of all the other participants. Consequently a carnivalesque narrative discourse is established through which the voices that yield to be dominant, which is mainly Mr. Ramsay’s voice, could not be established as a hierarchical position and even it loses its authoritative position as the other characters attend the dialogue in the context of the novel. The present article will take it to track the policies of dialogism and carnival in Woolf’s novel and to search the production of meaning via the emergence and development of these policies. The activity in it of dialogism is the cause of unfinalizability which is the vital feature of dialogism that allows the permanent operation of dialogue upon the course of time and prevents the establishment of hierarchical positions of power. The article will also take to extrapolate the different phases in the creation of this sense of dialogism in the novel and especially highlighting the role of Mrs. Ramsay in the fabrication of such a sense. Keywords : Bakhtin, Woolf, To the Light House , Dialogism, Carnivalesque, Unfinalizability

openalex_display_name: Solitudes imaginées : langues, romans nationaux et territoires littéraires au Québec
openalex_abstract: Les romans nationaux en anglais et en français au Québec mettent en scène un même espace littéraire. S’ils sont séparés en des territoires littéraires distincts, cela ne tient pas à des critères intrinsèques aux textes ou à leur imaginaire, mais bien à la nationalisation des corpus. Les histoires littéraires du XIXe siècle au Québec et au Canada ont d’abord fait reposer les frontières des corpus sur des bases ethniques et linguistiques, mais le nationalisme québécois a déplacé ces enjeux vers des questions territoriales au fil du XXe siècle, sans toutefois abandonner entièrement le référent ethnique. La lecture croisée de L’Appel de la race (1922) de Lionel Groulx et de Two Solitudes (1945) de Hugh MacLennan montre l’impasse des romans nationaux en anglais et en français dans leurs exclusions et leurs oppositions mutuelles avant la Révolution tranquille. Dans les années 1960, des romans comme Prochain Épisode (1965) d’Hubert Aquin et Beautiful Losers (1966) de Leonard Cohen tâchent de sortir de la dualité ethnique, mais restent aux prises avec les enjeux coloniaux qui l’ont imposée. Ces romans n’en comportent pas moins une similarité importante dans le territoire qu’ils imaginent réciproquement. La réinterprétation des mythes de fondation dans La Chaise du maréchal ferrant (1972) de Jacques Ferron et Solomon Gursky Was Here (1989) de Mordecai Richler permet de mieux comprendre comment les territorialisations créent un espace de tension dont l’horizon est la globalité. L’imaginaire des deux solitudes sert, par conséquent, à créer des corpus séparés artificiellement afin de correspondre à des nationalisations concurrentes de la littérature. Toutefois, cette thèse montre qu’il est possible, et même souhaitable, de penser ces cadres aux croisements des transferts et des catégories qui font de la littérature québécoise un espace en tension dont la portée ne devrait pas être limitée par la méthodologie de l’histoire littéraire. _____________________________________________________________________________ MOTS-CLÉS DE L’AUTEUR : Littérature anglo-québécoise, histoire croisée, nationalisme, roman national, territoire et territorialité, espace littéraire, Lionel Groulx, Hugh MacLennan, Hubert Aquin, Leonard Cohen, Jacques Ferron, Mordecai Richler

openalex_display_name: Writing, Men, Empire: Kipling’s Medievalist Imagination
openalex_abstract: In perhaps the best-crafted of his later short stories, “Dayspring Mishandled,” Rudyard Kipling transposes his readers back into the London of the early 1890s and presents them with a nostalgic glimpse of the loves of a group of young writers who gather once a week for supper at a popular café. All of them are talented and ambitious but impoverished and glad to write pot-boilers for the magazines of a new-style entrepreneur who supplies them with basic ideas, plot-outlines, and characters for the work. Among these young writers are the story’s protagonists, Manallace and Castorley. Castorley is a “mannered, bellied person” with a “high affected voice” and “gifts of waking dislike.” Manallace is “a darkish slow Northerner of the type that does not ignite but must be detonated.” On the occasion during which we meet both of them, Manallace admits that he has produced nothing for the syndicate this week. He had been given a batch of prints to weave a story around – stereotyped medieval subjects, “a knight, a castle, a young girl,” but they “have turned to poetry in his hands.” Only the narrator of the story, who takes the drunken Manallace home that night, learns that the poetry he was bragging about was Chaucerian verse. In a parallel development, Castorley leaves the syndicate. He has come into money and devotes himself to gentlemanly scholarship with Geoffrey Chaucer as his chosen subject. In their youth, both men had loved the same woman. She, however, La Bohème-style, had loved a third man, rejecting alike Castorley’s attempt to get her to bed and Manallace’s declaration of love. Castorley never forgives her and, when she becomes paralyzed, refuses to subscribe to a fund necessary for a vital operation. Manallace nurses her until her death in 1915. One night, when Manallace and Castorley are working together again in a government department during World War I, Castorley, in a confident mood, had spoken of the dead woman in terms that Kipling, probably for censorship reasons, cannot quote. Whatever Castorley said – Angus Wilson suggests that Kipling hints at the woman’s paralysis as being due to syphilis contracted by whoring – it suffices for Manallace to dedicate the rest of his life to exacting vengeance.

openalex_display_name: Building up Learners' Communicative Competence: the Politeness Principle
openalex_abstract: Learners of a second language may succeed in acquiring the linguistic competence of that language. However, the communicative competence is more important in social interaction with native speakers. Therefore, many principles are postulated for building up learners' communicative competence such as: the Cooperative Principle, the Politeness Principle and the Irony Principle (Leech, 1983). This paper will focus on one of these principles, i.e. the Politeness Principle and intends to answer the following questions: What is the Politeness Principle? What are the maxims and sub-maxims of the Politeness Principle? What is the relation between indirectness and politeness? Moreover, the Politeness Principle, together with its maxims and sub-maxims, will be applied to Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1894) to signify its role and importance in real life and to show how it works in face-to-face interaction. The paper concludes that the Politeness Principle is essential for learners to interpret indirect utterances in natural communication and dramatic dialogue, as well.

Self-Alienating Characters in the Fiction of John Steinbeck
openalex_abstract: The primary purpose of this study is to show that John Steinbeck's concern with alienation is pervasive and consistent from the beginning of his career as a writer until the end. The pervasiveness of his concern with alienation is demonstrated by examining his two early collections of short stories and by showing how alienated characters in these stories resemble alienated characters in all the author's major works of fiction. Since much confusion surrounds the meaning of the word "alienation," it is necessary to begin with a definition of "alienation" as it is used to discuss Steinbeck. An alienated character in Steinbeck's fiction is a person who is separated from another person, group of persons, society, or the person's ideal self. This study is concerned with characters who create their own alienation rather than with those who are merely helpless victims.

openalex_abstract: This essay focuses on Sophia Ripley’s 1841 article “Woman,” which was published in the Dial two years before Margaret Fuller’s “The Great Lawsuit. Man Versus Men. Woman Versus Women” appeared in the same publication. Originally written as homework for one of Fuller’s Boston Conversations (1839–1844), Ripley’s plea in favor of women’s right to education perfectly epitomizes the polyphonic nature of feminist social advances in antebellum America. Inspired by Fuller’s feminist reinterpretation of William Ellery Channing’s concept of “self-culture,” viewing education as a means to improve woman’s condition, Ripley’s text debunks the concept of “separate spheres” and urges readers to consider women as intellectual beings rather than through the prism of the idealized, unrealistic “muse.” Inscribing Ripley’s article as part of the feminist stride of the Transcendental movement, I will illustrate the similarities between Ripley’s argument, Fuller’s, and that of other women Transcendentalists, while also confronting it with what Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote on the subject.

openalex_display_name: Weaving Democracy
openalex_abstract: The lost thread of Jacques Rancière's title is an overdetermined signifier, itself an interwoven history. Most obviously, it refers to the loss of the authority of plot as derived from Aristotelian aesthetics. Aristotle redeemed literature from Plato's accusation of delusive falsehood by asserting that the artist's delineation of the rational chain of cause and effect was a superior form of truth to the historian's mere succession of facts. Subsequently, this order of rationality conferred the authority of its form of truth on philosophical and scientific discourse and on the social and political sciences. In the field of literature, rational verisimilitude produced a totalizing aesthetic in which only some people were designated capable of meaningful speech and action, dignified feelings, and motivation toward a noble goal. All those not privileged with the status of rationality were relegated to the order of noise rather than speech and their lives ruled by repetition as opposed to the heroic capacity for willed action.Much of Rancière's critical writing has delineated the destruction of this classical order of verisimilitude. The political, social, and aesthetic energies that constituted a turmoil of forces at the end of the eighteenth century overwhelmed the rational order of causal plot and its demarcation of who may and may not speak and act meaningfully. A new democratic aesthetic regime broke free in which anyone can say anything at all and in which any aspect of the world whatsoever became worthy of writing. Rancière claims that in place of the causal thread of plot as imposition of singular meaning and truth, a redistribution of sensible reality imposed itself. Instead of an idealist rational hierarchy, material existence comes to be understood as multiple, nonhierarchal, interwoven, and infinite. The rational thread of absolute truth is replaced by a plurality of verbal texture.Yet in many ways, Rancière's greater concern is with another loss. He argues that the aesthetic democratic revolution within literature has been misinterpreted by literary critics almost since its inception. Contemporary readers of early nineteenth-century realists criticized the mass of detail that flooded their texts as detrimental to aesthetic decorum. Subsequent critics, from Walter Benjamin to Roland Barthes, interpreted the new textual multiplicity of writing as a symptom of materialist excess, an obsessive compulsion to affirm the solidity of the bourgeois world as the only possible reality. The pursuit of art for art's sake was a means by which artists broke free from the claims of an overburdening materialism. Structuralist and poststructuralist writers likewise severed textuality from the sensible world. What gets completely lost in this long critical tradition of disdain for descriptive detail is recognition of the revolutionary potential of the aesthetic embrace of materiality. Rancière challenges this consensual judgment against physical matter. It is the excess of the sensible, he argues, that overthrows the old representational plot of action that had sustained classical verisimilitude. In its place an egalitarian inclusiveness and sensory inexhaustibility became, from the late eighteenth century, the defining quality of a new aesthetic regime.Undoubtedly, this is a revisionary account offering quite new ways of approaching realism and modernism, without a sense of binary opposition and without rejection of materialism. For Rancière, both realism and modernism need to be understood as participating in a democratic aesthetic that redistributes the perceptible world, ceaselessly expanding the horizons of the sensible. The structuring perception of the new aesthetic, replacing the linear drive of causality and action, is what Rancière terms the “lived fabric of a world,” an inclusive, interactive web of material reality (15). In The Lost Thread, he discusses the work of Flaubert, Conrad, and Woolf, whose narrative dynamics variously express a struggle for dominance between plot as imposition of hierarchical rationality, on one hand, and the unbounded textuality of a sensory realm on the other. In the second part of the book, Rancière analyzes the poetry of Keats and Baudelaire in terms of a republican aspiration of human creativity. A final essay on theater returns to the tension between political aspirations born of the revolutionary era and forms of artistic production. How is the new aesthetic dissensus to be expressed as understanding that can inform political thought and action without reinscribing it as a form of knowledge and thereby reinvesting in the tyranny of plot?Dissensus has been a central term in accounts of Rancière's writing, designating his focus upon points of fracture within political and aesthetic consensus. In particular, he argues that an egalitarian surge of sensory existence into the novel form around the end of the eighteenth century has its counterpart in the refusal of ordinary working people to stay within the scope of life and ambitions previously allotted them. The old consensuses of artistic decorum and social relations were both swept aside. In The Lost Thread, however, Rancière is somewhat less focused upon moments of dissensus than upon processes of transformational encounters between residual and revolutionary aesthetics. In his multifaceted analysis of texts, he seeks to uncover the political work of a new radical sensibility inherent in the form itself, regardless of content. While Emma Bovary's romantic dreams can be aligned with the aspirations of workers for emancipation from drudgery, the plot of Emma's story enacts no heroic enlargement. In general, while the new aesthetic regime is empowered by the sweep of multiple sensory reality into the textual life of art, Rancière argues, realist plots seal off democratic victories from their characters. Flaubert splits Emma into two aesthetic parts. One form of her imagined being enacts a condensation of the impersonal, teeming sensory fabric of life, the endless atoms of experience her body encounters. This is the verbal triumph of the new radical aesthetic; but the character knows her life only in terms of the old representative order, even while no longer retaining the freedom of heroic action. The nineteenth-century realists appropriated the egalitarian power of dissensus but sacrificed their characters to the plot, Rancière claims.Conrad shares the late nineteenth-century philosophical skepticism as to universal truths. Thus for him, the authority of plot is weakened. Conrad's stories, Rancière argues, arise from a mistaken assumption, illusion, or belief. The skepticism is textual in scope; the mass of verbal detail destroys the possibility of any final singular meaning. The texts of novels like Lord Jim enact a narrative decomposition into fragmented microscopic events. No finite resolution can limit the unending flow of a sensible world. But the novel as genre demands plot. In Lord Jim, an entirely arbitrary conclusion is simply imposed. In Heart of Darkness, Marlow's lie radically betrays Conrad's new egalitarian aesthetics of infinite textuality. The sheer magnitude of sensible existence that Conrad infuses into his stories and their distance from routine life preclude any ending commensurate with that vastness.Perhaps, Rancière suggests, the lesson is to shift the immensities of sky and space to the domestic sphere. Which is what Virginia Woolf does, he claims. All of Woolf's novels, he argues, articulate a tension between plot and a new aesthetic of nonexclusive multiplicity. The evocation of the radical otherness of sensible processes in the middle section of To the Lighthouse is curtailed by enclosure within the female plot of the first section and the father's plot in the final section. In Mrs. Dalloway, the dialectic between singularity and multiplicity is more integrated by means of anonymous subjectivities spread across city space. The narrative, likewise, disperses plot across multiple trajectories.Nevertheless, one might argue that Woolf's practice is more radical than Rancière recognizes. While Emma Bovary as character is split from consciousness of her being as sensory existence, Woolf's female characters inhabit that split as consciousness. They live simultaneously within the great democracy of the sensible world and within the consensual plots of power and subordination. As such they constitute a continuous force of dissensus throughout the text. Furthermore, far from domesticating the immensity of the sensible fabric of life, Woolf's verbal heterogeneity reconfigures consensual values of scale; material reality is a continuum encompassing atoms and stars, nerve fibers and tidal movement, discarded boots, traditional nursery rhymes, and the splatter of mud.Keats's engagement with the contentious politics of his time has long divided critical opinion: are his sympathies with radical causes or with the pursuit of an ideal of timeless beauty? Rancière's reading, focusing largely upon Ode to Autumn, argues that Keats's politics are inherent in his aesthetic practice. Rancière foregrounds the activity of art as weaving in opposition to the singularity of plot. Few poets, he claims, felt as powerfully as Keats that poetry is an interweaving of contraries: the material and the immaterial, passivity and activity. For Keats, the interwoven fabric that constitutes a poem brings into being a multiple community of existing poems, fragments of sound like birdsong, remembered images and words, and poems only entertained in reveries. This perception of the whole sensible fabric of existence underlying poetic sensibility projects a possible new human relationship of shared creativity. It is the form of egalitarian politics constituting Keats's verse. Keats's affirmation of negative capability refutes the traditional hierarchy in which only some are born to noble action and words and the many to mere existence. By refusing poetic individualism and annulling the difference between activity and reverie, Keats's poetic radicalism affirms a communal creativity unendingly interweaving all aspects of life. Keats thus participates in the great democratic upheavals, recognizing the capacity of the many to engage in the “diligent indolence” of art that will establish a community of equals (75).Baudelaire's radicalism, like that of Keats, inheres within his aesthetic practice, Rancière claims. Such a view directly challenges Benjamin's influential reading of Baudelaire. For such critics, Baudelaire gives powerful expression to the dehumanizing, sordid emptiness experienced by the fleeting crowds on city streets. His poetry voices alienation, not community. But Baudelaire's response is more complex, Rancière suggests, and derives from a Balzacian sense of human life so vast and varied that any Aristotelian rational causation founders. It is not so much that the modern world has become too prosaic as that it has become too immense to sustain plot. Baudelaire's poems enact encounters between subjects who are networks of sensation within a sensible world that has no limit.The poetic apprehension of this multiplicity requires a form of “reverie,” not as inwardness but as an erasure of any boundary between inside and outside. The poem is necessarily a fragment of this unstable, floating existence, a “patch of sky seen through the basement window” (105). As such, Baudelaire's verse sustains neither individualized Aristotelian subjectivity nor yet the singularity of pantheistic universal life. It is the multiplicity of sensible existence inhering in each glimpsed sight, each feeling, each momentary sensation of Baudelaire's poetic practice that offers itself, Rancière says, to “the aesthetic Republic's work of infinitization” (113). Baudelaire's complex response to the city recognizes its rapaciousness, its sordid appetites, but equally and positively grasps its poetic participation in a new democratic redistribution that erases the identifying boundaries of beauty, ugliness, sin, and grace. It is in the mutations, divisions, and contradictions of multiple life and multiple lives that “the idea of poetry and the Republic combined to draw a certain visage of community” (113).Rancière's account of the aesthetic transformations stemming from the revolutionary era brings a welcome challenge to the political skepticism that has dominated literary studies, especially in regard to realism. In that sense, his work is itself a project of dissensus, a redistribution of the perceptible of a new aesthetic regime. It is a regime that radically reconfigures the sensible world as an egalitarian, horizontal continuity beyond any possibility of completion. Neither is dissensus ever a completed project. The politics of aesthetics is not the acquiring of knowledge. It is a transformational redistributive practice. Thus Woolf shatters the consensual scale inscribing degrees of importance and relevance. Poets project a republican vision of creative community, sustained by a new sensibility of the infinite fabric of life. Within the current political world, across almost all consensual regimes, the plots of truth have hardened into hostile dogmas. One must hope that a sense of the multiply interwoven experiences, microevents, and epoch changes that constitute the material fabric of life will empower an aesthetic dissensus—not an Aristotelian realism but a recognition of the radical, egalitarian implications of inhabiting a shared sensory world, “the great democracy of sensible coexistences” (13).

openalex_display_name: Secret America: the CIA and American culture
openalex_abstract: Spying and writing have always gone together. In Britain, where the modern intelligence agency was born, intellectuals moved smoothly back and forth between secret government service and the literary life, some, like the journalist Malcolm Muggeridge, even spending the morning at the typewriter before consulting with MI6 after lunch. Somerset Maugham, Compton Mackenzie, Graham Greene, Ian Fleming, John Le Carré all placed their powers of observation and divination at the disposal of the British secret state while mining their experience of intelligence work in their fiction. It was not just a case of satisfying the reading public's apparently insatiable appetite for the espionage novel. There seemed to be some basic connection between the roles of writer and spy: both were iconic, even heroic figures in modern culture, necessarily detached from ordinary society, yet gifted - cursed, perhaps - with unique insight into the darkest realms of human existence. “I, from very early, lived a secret life, an inward life,” Le Carréonce told an interviewer. “I seemed to go about in disguise.” In this respect, the spies of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) were no different from their British counterparts. Indeed, the “man of letters” was, if anything, even more conspicuous a figure in the upper echelons of the American secret service than in MI6. During World War II, Norman Holmes Pearson, a noted Yale professor of literature and editor, alongside W. H. Auden, of the five-volume Viking Poets of the English Language , ran “X-2,” the London-based counterespionage branch of the Office of Strategic Services (OSS), the United States' wartime foreign intelligence agency.

openalex_display_name: XXVII. Antiquarian Interest in Elizabethan Drama Before Lamb
openalex_abstract: Charles Lamb, in the whimsical autobiographical sketch which he wrote in 1827, boasted that he “was the first to draw the public attention to the old English Dramatists, in a work called ‘Specimens of English Dramatic Writers,‘ who lived about the time of Shakespeare.” Lamb's first biographer, Talfourd, pictures the Specimens as slowly and almost imperceptibly working out “the genial purpose of the editor in renewing a taste for the great contemporaries of Shakespeare.” Ainger describes Lamb as a dispeller of ignorance and remarks of the Specimens: The very idea of the collection was a bold one… . With the one exception of Shakspeare, the dramatists of the period, between “the middle of Elizabeth's reign and the close of the reign of Charles I,” were unknown to the general reader of the year 1808?

openalex_display_name: 4. Middlemarch’s Brute Life
openalex_abstract: This chapter finds in both Charles Dickens’ Bleak House, and in Dickens’ several depictions of the slaughterhouses of London’s Smithfield Market, a concern with the possibility that whole, self-­possessed bodies will be processed and transformed into meat and other byproducts. In Bleak House, as elsewhere in Dickens, to be symbolically intimate with or proximate to animals – and especially to “follow” or “go after” them – is to fall into a state of questionable or precarious humanness or wholeness. These thematics recur throughout Dickens’ later work, as he frequently returns to a set of figures, images, and ideas relating to anxieties of dehumanization and fears of animalization. Great Expectations in particular exhibits a fear of being forgotten or misremembered, of “perishing out of all human knowledge,” a fate which Dickens specifically links to the state of being an animal, or of being animalized. This chapter suggests that Dickens’ very practices of characterization, and his definition of human characters and protagonists, should be understood in relation to his conception of the animal.

openalex_display_name: La fuerza de la sangre: la fugacidad del encuentro
openalex_abstract: Sin lugar a dudas, las conmemoraciones que hacen presente una vida o un acontecimiento se han encargado de impedir que el olvido se imponga sobre las hazanas alcanzadas por el ser humano en el mundo; bien sean estas de orden material o de caracter espiritual. Lo importante, como lo indica el acto de recordar, es conservar en la memoria a quienes con su grandeza han permitido que otros, de otras geografias y de otros tiempos, mantengan vigente su existencia, hasta el punto de volver a sus vidas, gracias, por ejemplo, a la pagina que no se borra o al relato que conserva la frescura de lo acabado de contar. Esto es lo que se intenta escribir y evocar de quien fuera el mas grande de las letras castellanas: Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, a los cuatrocientos anos de su muerte.
